abstract: This lecture covers the diagnosis and management of allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, and pharyngitis. Key points include proper use of intranasal glucocorticoids, antibiotic stewardship for sinusitis (10-day rule), and recognition of serious complications. The importance of differentiating viral from bacterial causes and avoiding unnecessary antibiotics is emphasized. Special attention is given to high-risk patients and appropriate treatment escalation.
key_points: Allergic rhinitis is IgE-mediated; nonallergic rhinitis is triggered by irritants like smoke or cold air.
First-line treatment for allergic rhinitis is intranasal fluticasone (Flonase) with proper technique (no inhalation needed).
For sinusitis, antibiotics are indicated only after 10 days of symptoms without improvement; exam findings alone are not sufficient.
Avoid macrolides (e.g., Z-Pak) for sinusitis due to poor efficacy.
High-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (2 g twice daily) is used for severe cases or risk factors (age >65, recent hospitalization, antibiotics in past month, immunocompromised, diabetes, CAD).
Montelukast carries a black box warning for neuropsychiatric events; use only in patients with asthma or when other treatments fail.
In pharyngitis, consider gonorrhea and chlamydia testing in patients with high-risk sexual behavior (MSM, oral sex).
Exam findings for allergic rhinitis include a transverse nasal crease and bluish turbinates.
Recurrent sinusitis requires 10 symptom-free days; if symptoms recur within 5 days of treatment, it is considered the same infection.
Complications of sinusitis (orbital cellulitis, osteomyelitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis) require imaging: CT for bone, MRI for soft tissue.
Use Centor criteria to determine who needs testing for strep throat; do not test if criteria are not met.
A negative rapid antigen test is reliable; do not routinely send a culture unless the patient is high risk.
